ic-38: Introduction to Insurance
Insurance is able to compensate the few who suffer a loss mainly because:
The insurer invests every premium only in government bonds
The government reimburses the insurer for every claim
The premiums of many people facing a similar risk are pooled to pay the losses of the few
Insured persons promise never to make a claim
Insurance works on pooling: many contribute small premiums so that the fund can pay the losses of the few who actually suffer them.
Introduction to Insurance
Which of the following risks is normally NOT insurable?
Loss from a fall in the price of shares an investor bought
Damage to a factory by fire
Death of the family breadwinner
Theft of goods from a warehouse
Insurance covers pure risks (only loss or no loss); a share-price fall is a speculative risk, which also carries a chance of gain and is not insurable.
Introduction to Insurance
A shop owner stops locking his store properly because he knows the stock is insured. This is an example of:
Physical hazard
Moral hazard
Peril
Speculative risk
Moral hazard is a change in the insured's attitude or behaviour (here, carelessness) that increases the chance of loss because insurance exists.
Introduction to Insurance
Buying an insurance policy is which risk-management technique?
Risk avoidance
Risk retention
Loss prevention
Risk transfer
By paying a premium the individual transfers the financial consequence of the risk to the insurer.
Customer Service & Grievances
Under IRDAI's 2024 policyholder-protection framework, the free-look period for life and health insurance policies is:
7 days from the date of proposal
15 days from the date of the first premium
30 days from receipt of the policy document
45 days from the risk commencement date
IRDAI's 2024 regulations extended the free-look period to 30 days from receipt of the policy document for life and health policies.
Customer Service & Grievances
Before a policyholder can file a complaint with the Insurance Ombudsman, he or she must normally:
File a civil suit in the district court
Get written approval from the insurance agent
Obtain a no-objection certificate from IRDAI
First complain in writing to the insurer and be rejected, get no reply in the prescribed time, or be dissatisfied with the reply
The Ombudsman is an appellate forum for grievances: the insurer must first be given the chance to resolve the complaint.
Customer Service & Grievances
Bima Bharosa is best described as:
A government scheme that guarantees all insurance claims
A crop insurance scheme for small farmers
The licensing portal through which agents pay their fees
IRDAI's online platform for registering and tracking grievances against insurers
Bima Bharosa (the successor to IGMS) is IRDAI's integrated grievance management system for policyholder complaints.
Customer Service & Grievances
An agent who looks at a customer as a source of repeat business, referrals and renewals over many years is focusing on:
One-time sales incentive
Moral hazard
Customer lifetime value
Adverse selection
Customer lifetime value is the value of all business a customer may bring over the whole relationship, which rewards good long-term service.
Regulatory Aspects of Agency
Section 41 of the Insurance Act, 1938 prohibits:
Offering a rebate of commission or premium as an inducement to take a policy
Nomination by the policyholder
Assignment of a policy to a bank
Payment of premium by cheque
Section 41 bars allowing or offering any rebate as an inducement to take or renew insurance; the agent cannot share commission with the customer.
Regulatory Aspects of Agency
Under Section 64VB of the Insurance Act, an insurer cannot assume a risk unless:
The agent has visited the proposer's home
The policy has been in force for one year
The proposer has submitted an income-tax return
The premium is received in advance (or guaranteed / deposited in the prescribed manner)
Section 64VB requires premium to be received in advance before the insurer assumes risk, so cover starts only after payment.
Regulatory Aspects of Agency
Under the framework after the 2015 amendment to the Insurance Act, an individual insurance agent is appointed by:
IRDAI directly, through a licence issued to the individual
The Ministry of Finance
The insurer, following IRDAI's eligibility, training and examination norms
The Insurance Ombudsman
Since the 2015 amendment, insurers appoint agents under IRDAI-approved policies; IRDAI sets the qualification and exam requirements.
Regulatory Aspects of Agency
Which of the following actions by an agent violates the code of conduct?
Explaining all benefits and exclusions of a plan
Persuading a policyholder to let an existing policy lapse so that a new one can be sold
Disclosing the agent's identity and the insurer represented
Helping the claimant complete claim forms
Inducing a customer to discontinue an existing policy to buy a new one (twisting) harms the policyholder and is prohibited.
Legal Principles of Insurance
The principle of utmost good faith requires:
Both proposer and insurer to voluntarily disclose all material facts accurately
Only the insurer to disclose its financial results
The proposer to disclose facts only if specifically asked
The agent to guarantee the claim amount
Insurance contracts are uberrimae fidei: each party must disclose all material facts, whether asked or not.
Legal Principles of Insurance
In life insurance, insurable interest must exist:
Only at the time of claim
At the time the policy is taken
Both at inception and at the time of claim
At no stage, since life insurance is a gift
For life insurance, insurable interest is required at inception; it need not continue until death (e.g., after divorce).
Legal Principles of Insurance
Which principle does NOT apply to a life insurance policy?
Utmost good faith
Insurable interest
Valid consideration
Indemnity
Human life cannot be valued exactly, so a life policy pays the agreed sum assured; it is a contract of assurance, not indemnity (hence no contribution or subrogation).
Legal Principles of Insurance
A building is insured with Insurer A for ₹4 lakh and Insurer B for ₹6 lakh. A fire causes a loss of ₹2 lakh. Under contribution, Insurer A will pay:
Rateable share = 4/(4+6) × ₹2,00,000 = ₹80,000; Insurer B pays the remaining ₹1,20,000.
Legal Principles of Insurance
For a valid insurance contract the parties must be competent. Who among these is NOT competent to contract on his own?
A 25-year-old salaried employee
A 60-year-old retired teacher
A 40-year-old businesswoman
A 16-year-old proposing for a policy on his own life
Under the Indian Contract Act a minor (below 18) cannot enter a valid contract, so a proposal must be made by a guardian or adult.
Life Insurance & Financial Planning
Using the income-capitalisation method, what is the Human Life Value of a person who contributes ₹4,80,000 a year to the family if the assumed interest rate is 8%?
HLV = annual contribution ÷ interest rate = ₹4,80,000 ÷ 0.08 = ₹60,00,000, the sum that would yield the same income.
Life Insurance & Financial Planning
Using the Rule of 72, money invested at 9% per annum will roughly double in:
6 years
9 years
12 years
8 years
Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ rate = 72 ÷ 9 = 8 years.
Life Insurance & Financial Planning
For a young married earner with small children and a home loan, the top insurance priority is usually:
A single-premium pension plan
Adequate pure term cover to protect the family's income
A short-term travel policy
An immediate annuity
At this life stage dependants rely on the earner's income, so high protection at low cost (term insurance) is the main need.
Life Insurance Products
A pure term insurance plan typically:
Pays the sum assured on survival to maturity
Pays the sum assured only if the insured dies during the policy term
Guarantees bonuses every year
Has a compulsory five-year lock-in
Term insurance is pure protection; if the insured survives the term, nothing is payable (unless it is a return-of-premium variant).
Life Insurance Products
The minimum lock-in period for a Unit Linked Insurance Plan (ULIP) is:
5 years
1 year
3 years
10 years
IRDAI rules lock ULIP funds for five years; discontinued policies move to a discontinuance fund until the lock-in ends.
Life Insurance Products
An endowment assurance policy pays the sum assured:
On death during the term or on survival to the end of the term, whichever is earlier
Only on death during the term
Only after the insured reaches age 100
Only if the insured becomes disabled
Endowment combines protection and savings: the benefit is paid on earlier death or at maturity.
Life Insurance Products
In a money-back policy, if the insured dies after receiving two survival benefits, the nominee usually gets:
Only the balance after deducting survival benefits paid
Only the premiums paid without interest
The full sum assured (plus applicable bonus), without deduction of survival benefits already paid
Nothing, because survival benefits were already paid
Money-back plans pay periodic survival benefits, but the full death benefit is payable on death within the term regardless of earlier payouts.
Life Insurance Products
An annuity mainly protects a person against:
The risk of dying too early
The risk of outliving one's savings (living too long)
Damage to property
Hospitalisation expenses
An annuity converts a corpus into a regular income for life, addressing longevity risk.
Pricing & Valuation
The office (gross) premium of a life policy is:
Net premium plus loadings for expenses, contingencies and (for with-profit plans) bonus
Net premium minus the agent's commission
Only the mortality cost of the year
The sum assured divided by the term
Net premium covers mortality and interest; loadings for expenses and other margins are added to arrive at the office premium.
Pricing & Valuation
If an actuary assumes a higher rate of interest on invested premiums, other factors remaining the same, the premium will:
Decrease
Increase
Remain unchanged
Become equal to the sum assured
Higher assumed investment earnings mean less premium is needed today to fund the future benefit, so premiums fall.
Pricing & Valuation
Life insurers in India price and value policies using mortality tables known as:
Consumer Price Index tables
National Sample Survey tables
Life Insurance Penetration tables
Indian Assured Lives Mortality (IALM) tables
IALM tables, built from insured lives' experience in India, are the standard base for mortality assumptions.
Documentation & Underwriting
The primary document on which a life insurance contract is based is the:
Proposal form
Premium receipt
Agent's report only
Claim form
The proposal form carries the proposer's declarations and is the foundation of the contract; misstatements in it can affect claims.
Documentation & Underwriting
Which of the following is generally treated as a STANDARD age proof?
Self-declaration of age
Horoscope
School leaving certificate
Village elders' certificate
Standard age proofs are official records such as birth or school certificates and passports; self-declarations are non-standard.
Documentation & Underwriting
A policy taken under Section 6 of the Married Women's Property Act, 1874 for the benefit of wife and children:
Creates a trust, so the policy money cannot be attached by the policyholder's creditors
Can be surrendered freely by the husband for his own use
Must be assigned to the insurer
Can be nominated in favour of a friend
An MWPA policy is held in trust for the named beneficiaries and is outside the reach of the policyholder's creditors or control.
Documentation & Underwriting
Under Section 45 of the Insurance Act, an insurer cannot call a life policy in question on any ground after:
One year from issue
Three years from the date of the policy, revival or rider, whichever is later
Five years from issue
Ten years from issue
Section 45 makes a policy indisputable after three years, protecting policyholders against late repudiation.
Documentation & Underwriting
In underwriting a substandard life, a 'lien' means:
The premium is waived for the first year
The policy is issued without medical tests
The sum assured payable is reduced if death occurs within a specified early period
The nominee is changed to the insurer
A lien temporarily reduces the death benefit in early years to offset a higher, decreasing extra risk.
Documentation & Underwriting
Under Section 39 as amended in 2015, which nominee is a 'beneficial nominee' entitled to the policy money in their own right?
The policyholder's friend
The policyholder's spouse
The policyholder's employer
The policyholder's cousin
Parents, spouse and children (or any of them) nominated are beneficial nominees; others merely receive the money as trustees for the legal heirs.
Documentation & Underwriting
When a life policy is absolutely assigned under Section 38 (other than to the insurer for a policy loan), the existing nomination:
Continues to remain valid
Is automatically cancelled
Passes to the assignee's spouse
Becomes a joint nomination
Assignment transfers rights to the assignee, so an existing nomination is cancelled except where assignment is to the insurer against a loan.
Life Insurance Claims
A policy has sum assured ₹5,00,000 with 20 annual premiums. After paying 8 premiums the policyholder stops paying; accrued bonus is ₹40,000. The paid-up value is:
Life Insurance Claims
Insurers usually investigate a death claim more closely when death occurs:
After the maturity date
After 15 years of continuous premium payment
Within three years of the policy or revival (an early claim)
Only when the nominee is the spouse
Early claims, within the period in which Section 45 allows contesting the policy, are checked for non-disclosure or fraud.
Life Insurance Claims
If the life assured has been missing and not heard of for a continuous period, the law presumes death after:
1 year
3 years
7 years
12 years
Indian evidence law allows a presumption of death if a person has not been heard of for seven years; claimants usually need a court decree.
Health Insurance
A hospitalisation claim admissible at ₹1,50,000 is subject to a 10% co-payment. The insurer will pay:
Co-pay of 10% = ₹15,000 is borne by the insured; insurer pays 1,50,000 − 15,000 = ₹1,35,000.
Health Insurance
Following IRDAI's 2024 health insurance reforms, the maximum waiting period that can be applied to pre-existing diseases is:
12 months
48 months
60 months
36 months
IRDAI's 2024 health master circular cut the maximum waiting period for pre-existing diseases from four years to three years (36 months).
Health Insurance
A top-up policy has a deductible of ₹3 lakh and sum insured ₹10 lakh. For a single admissible claim of ₹5 lakh, the top-up insurer pays:
₹5 lakh
₹3 lakh
₹2 lakh
Nothing
The top-up pays only the amount above the deductible: 5 − 3 = ₹2 lakh.
Health Insurance
A cumulative bonus in a health policy means:
A cash payment at the end of each year
An increase in sum insured for each claim-free year without extra premium
A discount on the agent's commission
Refund of all premiums at policy end
Insurers reward claim-free years by raising the sum insured (within limits) at no extra cost.
Health Insurance
A Third Party Administrator (TPA) in health insurance:
Decides the premium rates for all insurers
Acts as the policyholder's legal advocate
Underwrites and bears the risk itself
Provides services such as cashless authorisation and claim processing on behalf of the insurer
TPAs are IRDAI-registered service providers who handle claim services for insurers; the risk stays with the insurer.
Health Insurance
Health insurance portability allows a policyholder to:
Move to another insurer while retaining credit for waiting periods already served
Transfer the policy to a relative
Convert the policy into a life policy
Claim from two insurers for the same bill amount twice
Portability protects continuity: waiting periods completed with the earlier insurer are credited by the new insurer up to the earlier sum insured.
Health Insurance
Which of the following is generally covered under a standard personal accident policy?
Hospitalisation for typhoid
Permanent total disablement caused by a road accident
Death due to heart disease
Treatment for diabetes
Personal accident cover pays for death or disablement caused solely by accidental, external and visible means, not illness.
General Insurance
A house worth ₹10 lakh is insured for ₹6 lakh under a policy with an average clause. A fire causes a loss of ₹4 lakh. The claim payable is:
Under-insurance applies: claim = loss × SI/value = 4,00,000 × 6/10 = ₹2,40,000.
General Insurance
Third-party liability cover for motor vehicles plying in public places is compulsory under:
The Insurance Act, 1938
The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988
The Consumer Protection Act, 2019
The Indian Contract Act, 1872
The Motor Vehicles Act mandates third-party cover; own-damage cover is optional.
General Insurance
The Insured Declared Value (IDV) of a private car is based on:
The price the owner hopes to sell the car for
The manufacturer's listed selling price less depreciation as per the prescribed schedule
The amount of the car loan outstanding
The total premiums paid since purchase
IDV is the sum insured for own damage, computed from the listed price adjusted for age-based depreciation.
General Insurance
A No Claim Bonus (NCB) in motor insurance:
Is a cash reward paid to the driver each year
Increases the third-party premium
Belongs to the vehicle and stays with it on sale
Is a discount on own-damage premium for claim-free years and is usually lost when a claim is made
NCB rewards claim-free renewals with an own-damage premium discount; it belongs to the insured, not the vehicle, and is forfeited on a claim.
General Insurance
In marine cargo insurance, insurable interest must exist:
At the time of loss
Only at the time of proposal
Only on the date of shipment
At no time, as cargo is always insured
Since cargo changes hands during transit, marine law requires the insured to have insurable interest when the loss occurs.
ncfm-cmd: Investors trade already-listed shares among themselves
Securities are issued by the company for the first time (or additionally) to raise capital
The primary market is the new-issue market where funds flow to the issuer; existing securities trade in the secondary market.
The Nifty 50 index is calculated using the:
Full market capitalisation including promoter shares
Nifty weights stocks by market value of shares freely available for trading, excluding promoter and locked-in holdings.
Cancelling shares bought back by a company
Converting physical share certificates into electronic holdings in a depository account
Converting shares into cash on sale
Demat holdings are electronic book entries with a depository, eliminating risks of physical certificates.
An equity shareholder has a claim on the company's profits and assets that is:
Fixed at a guaranteed rate of interest
Limited to the dividend declared in the first year
Residual, i.e., after the claims of creditors and preference shareholders are met
Equity owners bear the most risk and receive what remains after all prior claims, which is why equity returns are not guaranteed.
A bulk deal is a transaction where the total quantity traded by a client in a scrip in a day exceeds:
0.5% of the number of equity shares of the company listed
Exchanges disclose bulk deals where a client's total traded quantity exceeds 0.5% of the listed shares in a day.
The two depositories in India are:
National Securities Depository Ltd and Central Depository Services (India) Ltd hold securities in electronic form.
An investor opens a demat account through a:
Depository Participants (banks, brokers etc.) act as agents of the depository and provide account services to investors.
Foreign portfolio investors typically use a custodian to:
Hold their securities in safekeeping and handle settlement and corporate-action services
Fix the issue price of IPOs
Act as market makers on the exchange
Custodians provide safekeeping, settlement and related services for institutional clients.
A Professional Clearing Member (PCM) is one who:
Only trades for its own account without clearing
Clears and settles trades executed by other trading members but does not trade itself
Issues shares on behalf of companies
PCMs (often banks/custodians) undertake clearing and settlement for trading members or custodial participants without trading rights.
After SEBI's rationalisation (2018), existing sub-brokers had to either become trading members or migrate to the category of:
SEBI merged the sub-broker category into Authorised Persons, who act as agents of a trading member.
The purpose of the Unique Client Code (UCC) is to:
Identify each client uniquely so that orders and trades are tagged to the correct client
Every order must carry the client's UCC (linked to PAN) for audit trail, surveillance and risk control.
A trading member must issue a contract note to the client:
Within 24 hours of execution of the trade
Only at the end of the month
Only when the client requests it
SEBI requires contract notes (physical or electronic) within 24 hours of the trade.
Under SEBI's running-account norms, unless the client opts otherwise, a broker must settle the client's unused funds:
At least once every quarter (or monthly, if the client chooses)
Only when the account is closed
Only after the financial year ends
Brokers must return unused client funds through periodic (quarterly or monthly) running-account settlement.
Which of the following is permitted for a trading member?
Using one client's funds to meet another client's obligations
Keeping client funds in a separate client bank account
Using client funds for its proprietary trades
Pledging client securities for its own borrowing
Client funds and securities must be segregated and used only for that client's obligations.
Orders in NSE's trading system are matched on the basis of:
The best-priced order gets priority; among orders at the same price, the earlier one is matched first.
Among outstanding buy orders for a stock, the 'best' buy order is the one with the:
Buyers willing to pay more get priority; for sell orders the lowest price is best.
The order book has buy orders at ₹201 (entered first), ₹202 (entered second) and ₹200 (entered third). A new sell limit order at ₹200 arrives. It will first match with:
The buy order at ₹202, at a trade price of ₹202
The best (highest) buy order is matched first, and the trade occurs at the price of the passive order already in the book, i.e., ₹202.
A stop-loss sell order has a trigger price of ₹95 and limit price of ₹94. It means:
The share is sold immediately at ₹95
When the last traded price reaches ₹95, the order is released as a sell limit order at ₹94
The order is cancelled if the price reaches ₹95
It becomes a buy order at ₹94
A stop-loss order stays inactive until the trigger price is hit, then enters the book as a limit order at the specified limit price.
Remains in the system until the end of the day
Is executed only in the closing session
Is executed to the extent possible as soon as it is released, and any unmatched portion is cancelled
Can be modified throughout the day
IOC orders do not rest in the book: whatever is not filled immediately is cancelled.
On NSE, the disclosed quantity for an order must be at least:
Disclosed quantity lets a trader reveal only part of a large order, subject to a minimum of 10% of the total order.
The normal market session for equities on NSE runs from:
Pre-open call auction runs 9:00–9:15 and continuous normal-market trading is from 9:15 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.
In the pre-open call auction, the equilibrium (opening) price is the price at which:
The previous day's closing price is repeated
The highest buy order was placed
The maximum quantity can be traded
Call auctions discover a single price that maximises matched volume, reducing opening volatility.
Index-based market-wide circuit breakers in India are triggered at index movements of:
A movement of 10%, 15% or 20% in Nifty 50 or Sensex triggers a coordinated trading halt across the market.
A market order is one that:
Is executed only at the closing price
Becomes active only on hitting a trigger price
Is executed at the best price available in the order book at that time
Market orders carry no price limit and take the best available counter-price, giving speed but not price certainty.
The standard settlement cycle for equity trades in India's cash market is:
India completed migration to T+1 rolling settlement for all listed equities in January 2023.
Novation by a clearing corporation means it:
Becomes the legal counterparty – buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer
Rejects trades above a certain value
Nets only trades of the same client
Charges an extra fee for settlement
Novation substitutes the clearing corporation as central counterparty, removing bilateral counterparty risk.
A member, on its proprietary account, buys 500 shares of X at ₹100 and sells 300 shares of X at ₹102 on the same day. After netting, it must:
Net shares = 500 − 300 = 200 to receive; funds = 50,000 − 30,600 = ₹19,400 payable.
The clearing corporation of the National Stock Exchange is:
NSE Clearing Ltd (formerly NSCCL) clears and settles trades on NSE; ICCL is BSE's clearing corporation.
When a selling member fails to deliver shares on the pay-in day, the clearing corporation generally:
Cancels the trade without any charge
Asks the buyer to wait until the seller buys shares
Pays the buyer the previous day's closing price only
Conducts an auction to buy the shares, and closes out if the auction fails
Short deliveries are met through the auction mechanism; if shares cannot be bought, the position is closed out at a prescribed price.
'Pay-in' in clearing and settlement refers to:
Members delivering funds and securities to the clearing corporation
The clearing corporation releasing funds and securities to members
Pay-in is members' delivery of obligations to the CC; pay-out is the CC's release to receiving members.
The Core Settlement Guarantee Fund maintained by a clearing corporation is meant to:
Compensate investors for poor investment returns
Ensure timely completion of settlement even if a clearing member defaults
The Core SGF backs the CC's settlement guarantee so that non-defaulting members are not affected by a default.
Under the T+1 settlement cycle, the ex-date for a corporate action such as a dividend is:
One day after the record date
Two days before the record date
The same day as the record date
Five days before the record date
With T+1, a purchase made a day before the record date settles on the record date, so the ex-date coincides with the record date.
VaR margin in the cash market is designed to cover:
All possible losses under any circumstances
The largest loss expected on most days (a high, e.g. 99%, confidence level) over a one-day horizon
VaR margin covers potential one-day losses at a high confidence level; extreme losses beyond it are covered by ELM.
A client bought 200 shares at ₹450. The day's closing price is ₹438. The mark-to-market loss is:
For a trade value of ₹5,00,000, VaR margin is 12% and extreme loss margin is 3.5%. The total of these margins is:
The Extreme Loss Margin (ELM) is collected to cover:
Losses beyond those captured by VaR margin in extreme market conditions
ELM is an additional buffer for tail events that VaR does not capture.
A stock has a 5% price band and its previous close is ₹400. Orders can be placed within the range of:
Under SEBI's margin framework, brokers must collect margins from clients:
Only at the end of the settlement week
Upfront, before or at the time of the trade, with shortfalls attracting penalty
Only if the client makes a loss
Upfront and peak-margin rules require margins to be collected in advance; shortfalls are penalised.
Recognition of stock exchanges in India is governed by the:
SCRA 1956 provides for recognition of stock exchanges and regulation of contracts in securities.
SEBI was given statutory powers by the:
Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992
SEBI was set up in 1988 and became a statutory regulator under the SEBI Act, 1992.
A company official trades in the company's shares while aware of an unannounced merger. This is an example of:
Insider trading on unpublished price-sensitive information
SEBI's insider trading regulations prohibit dealing while in possession of UPSI such as an unannounced merger.
Under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, intermediaries report suspicious transactions to:
FIU-IND is the central agency receiving STRs and other reports under PMLA.
The legal framework for depositories and electronic holding of securities in India is provided by the:
The Depositories Act, 1996 enabled dematerialisation and electronic transfer of securities.
SEBI's online platform for investors to lodge and track complaints against listed companies and intermediaries
SCORES (SEBI Complaints Redress System) lets investors file grievances and monitor their resolution online.

A share priced at ₹150 pays an annual dividend of ₹6. Its dividend yield is:
Expected dividend next year is ₹5, required return is 13% and dividends grow at 8% forever. The share's value by the constant-growth model is:
What is the present value of ₹1,10,250 receivable after 2 years if the discount rate is 5% compounded annually?
A company has net worth of ₹200 crore and 4 crore shares; the share trades at ₹75. Its price-to-book ratio is:
Return on Equity (ROE) is calculated as:
Net profit after tax ÷ shareholders' equity
ROE measures profit earned for each rupee of shareholders' funds.
jaiib: Fiscal deficit of the government is:
Total expenditure minus total receipts including borrowings
Total expenditure minus (revenue receipts plus non-debt capital receipts)
Fiscal deficit measures the total borrowing requirement: expenditure not covered by revenue and non-debt capital receipts.
GDP at market prices is ₹250 lakh crore, indirect taxes are ₹30 lakh crore and subsidies ₹10 lakh crore. GDP at factor cost is:
Factor cost = market price − net indirect taxes = 250 − (30 − 10) = ₹230 lakh crore.
The Monetary Policy Committee of RBI consists of:
Four members, with the Finance Secretary as chair
Six members, with the Governor having a casting vote in case of a tie
The MPC has three RBI members (including the Governor, who chairs) and three external members; the Governor has a casting vote.
Under India's flexible inflation targeting framework, the CPI inflation target is:
The government has set the target at 4% CPI inflation, with an upper limit of 6% and lower limit of 2%.
In RBI's liquidity adjustment framework, if the policy repo rate is 6.00%, the Marginal Standing Facility rate is:
MSF is set 25 basis points above the repo rate (and SDF 25 bps below), so MSF = 6.25%.
Maintained by banks as cash balances with RBI, on which no interest is paid
Held by banks in gold in their own vaults
Lent to NBFCs at the repo rate
CRR is a share of net demand and time liabilities kept as balances with RBI and earns no interest.
Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) can be maintained in the form of:
Cash, gold and unencumbered approved securities held by the bank
Fixed deposits with other banks only
SLR assets are liquid assets like cash, gold and approved government securities, maintained by the bank itself.
Treasury bills in India are currently issued with maturities of:
The Government of India issues T-bills of 91-day, 182-day and 364-day tenors through RBI auctions.
Commercial Paper in India can be issued for a maturity of:
Minimum 7 days and maximum one year
RBI directions allow CP tenors from 7 days up to one year from the date of issue.
The regulator for the National Pension System is:
The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority regulates NPS and pension funds.
The apex development financial institution for agriculture and rural development in India is:
NABARD finances and supervises rural credit institutions and promotes agricultural development; SIDBI serves MSMEs.
Foreign Direct Investment inflows into India are recorded in the Balance of Payments under the:
FDI creates claims on assets/liabilities and is a capital account item; trade and remittances are current account items.
When RBI purchases government securities through open market operations, it:
Injects liquidity into the banking system
Absorbs liquidity from the banking system
RBI pays banks for the securities, adding to their reserves and increasing liquidity.
With respect to a savings bank deposit, the relationship between the bank and the customer is primarily that of:
The bank owes the deposited money to the customer, so the bank is the debtor and the depositor the creditor.
Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, after a cheque is dishonoured for insufficient funds, the payee must send a written demand notice to the drawer within:
30 days of receiving information of dishonour
The payee must issue notice within 30 days; the drawer then gets 15 days to pay before a complaint can be filed.
As per RBI instructions, banks should not pay cheques presented after:
One month from the date of the cheque
Three months from the date of the cheque
Six months from the date of the cheque
One year from the date of the cheque
Cheques become stale after three months from their date and are returned unpaid.
A cheque crossed 'Account Payee' should be:
Collected only for credit to the account of the named payee
Paid in cash across the counter
Endorsed to any third party freely
The account payee crossing directs the collecting banker to credit the proceeds only to the payee's account.
A banker's general lien is often described as:
An implied pledge, as the bank can sell the goods/securities after reasonable notice
A guarantee by a third party
Unlike an ordinary lien (only retention), a banker's lien carries an implied power of sale, so it is called an implied pledge.
A garnishee order received by a bank is:
An instruction from the customer to stop payment
A notice from RBI to freeze all accounts
An order to open a new account
A court order attaching the money of a judgement-debtor held by the bank
The bank (garnishee) must stop payment of the attached funds and hold them as directed by the court.
Under RBI's KYC directions, periodic updation of KYC for a high-risk customer must be done at least once every:
Re-KYC is required every 2 years for high-risk, 8 years for medium-risk and 10 years for low-risk customers.
A term loan becomes a non-performing asset when interest or instalment remains overdue for more than:
Under RBI's IRAC norms, a term loan is an NPA if interest/instalment is overdue for more than 90 days.
A secured loan of ₹20 lakh has been classified as substandard. At the general provisioning rate of 15%, the provision required is:

A customer's savings account has a credit balance of ₹50,000 and his personal loan in the same name and capacity has ₹80,000 overdue. The bank's right to adjust the deposit against the overdue loan is called the:
Set-off lets a bank combine accounts of the same customer held in the same capacity to recover a debt that has become due, ordinarily after notice to the customer.
A 'holder in due course' under the Negotiable Instruments Act is one who obtains the instrument:
For consideration, in good faith, before it became due, without reason to doubt the transferor's title
As a gift from the drawer
By finding it on the road
These conditions give a holder in due course a better title, free from defects of prior parties.
Statutory protection to a collecting banker who collects a crossed cheque in good faith and without negligence is provided by:
Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act
Section 131 of the Negotiable Instruments Act
Section 5 of the Banking Regulation Act
Section 131 protects the collecting banker from liability to the true owner if it acted in good faith and without negligence.
Which of the following deposits is NOT covered by DICGC deposit insurance?
Fixed deposits of a proprietorship firm
Recurring deposits of a salaried person
DICGC excludes deposits of foreign governments, central/state governments, inter-bank deposits and certain others.
₹1,00,000 is invested at 10% per annum compounded annually. The amount after 2 years is:
The effective annual rate of a 12% nominal rate compounded quarterly is approximately:
A machine costs ₹1,00,000, has a scrap value of ₹10,000 and a useful life of 5 years. Annual depreciation under the straight-line method is:
An asset costing ₹1,00,000 is depreciated at 20% on the written-down value method. Depreciation for the second year is:
A firm has current assets of ₹6 lakh and current liabilities of ₹4 lakh. Its current ratio is:
Fixed costs are ₹2,00,000, selling price is ₹50 per unit and variable cost is ₹30 per unit. The break-even quantity is:
BEP = fixed cost ÷ contribution per unit = 2,00,000 ÷ (50 − 30) = 10,000 units.
A bond of face value ₹100 with an 8% annual coupon is trading at ₹80. Its current yield is:
The main purpose of preparing a trial balance is to:
Find the market value of assets
Check the arithmetical accuracy of ledger postings
A trial balance verifies that total debits equal total credits; it cannot reveal errors such as errors of principle or compensating errors.
While reconciling, a firm finds cheques issued to suppliers but not yet presented for payment. As a result, the balance as per the bank passbook will be:
Higher than the balance as per the cash book
Lower than the balance as per the cash book
Equal to the balance as per the cash book
The cash book is credited when cheques are issued, but the bank has not yet debited them, so the passbook shows a higher balance.
A project costs ₹1,000 and returns ₹600 at the end of each of the next two years. At a discount rate of 10%, its NPV is approximately:
A project costing ₹5,00,000 generates an even cash inflow of ₹1,25,000 per year. Its payback period is:
In India, the quote 'USD 1 = ₹84.00' is an example of a:
A direct quote expresses the price of one unit of foreign currency in home currency; India uses direct quotes.
Under RBI norms, the maximum loan-to-value ratio for an individual housing loan up to ₹30 lakh is:
LTV caps are 90% for loans up to ₹30 lakh, 80% for above ₹30 lakh up to ₹75 lakh, and 75% above ₹75 lakh.
In a standard reducing-balance EMI loan, the early instalments consist of:
A larger interest component and a smaller principal component
Equal principal and interest every month
A smaller interest component than later instalments
Interest is charged on the outstanding balance, which is highest early, so early EMIs are mostly interest.
Credit Information Companies (such as those producing credit scores) in India are governed by the:
CICRA 2005 regulates credit bureaus, which collect credit data and generate credit reports and scores.
For a 28-year-old investor with a long investment horizon and high risk tolerance, an adviser would ordinarily recommend:
A relatively higher allocation to equity
Investing everything in savings bank deposits
Long horizons allow equity volatility to average out, so higher equity exposure suits young, risk-tolerant investors.
An investor puts ₹1,200 each month into a mutual fund through SIP at NAVs of ₹10, ₹12 and ₹15. The average cost per unit is:
Units = 120 + 100 + 80 = 300 for ₹3,600; average cost = 3,600 ÷ 300 = ₹12, lower than the average NAV of ₹12.33 (rupee-cost averaging).
Which feature best characterises retail banking?
A large number of customers with relatively small, standardised transactions
A few large corporate borrowers with customised loans
Only foreign exchange trading for exporters
Retail banking serves individuals and small businesses with mass-market products such as deposits, cards and personal loans.
The first step in the financial planning process for a client is to:
Establish the client–planner relationship and define its scope
Planning begins by defining the engagement, followed by gathering data, analysis, recommendations, implementation and monitoring.
A reverse mortgage loan is designed for:
Senior citizens who own a house and want periodic payments against it
The senior citizen continues living in the house and receives payments; the loan is settled from the property later.
On a credit card, the interest-free period on purchases is generally available only if the cardholder:
Pays only the minimum amount due
Pays after the due date with late fee
Pays the total amount due in full by the payment due date
If only part of the bill is paid, interest is charged on purchases from the transaction date and the free credit period is lost.
When a bank sells insurance policies to its customers as a corporate agent of an insurer, it is called:
Bancassurance uses the bank's branch network and customer base to distribute insurance products.
Unified Payments Interface (UPI) is operated by:
NPCI, an RBI-promoted umbrella organisation, operates UPI along with IMPS, RuPay and other retail payment systems.
A borrower earns ₹1,00,000 a month and already pays EMIs of ₹15,000. If the bank caps the fixed obligations to income ratio (FOIR) at 50%, the maximum new EMI allowed is:
caiib: The population variance of the observations 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 is:
Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation always lies between:
Correlation is a bounded measure: +1 is perfect positive, −1 perfect negative and 0 no linear relationship.
For an even number of ordered values, median = average of the middle two = (9 + 12) ÷ 2 = 10.5.
Two fair coins are tossed. The probability of getting at least one head is:
P(no head) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4, so P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.
In a normal distribution, approximately what share of observations lie within one standard deviation of the mean?
The empirical rule: about 68% within ±1σ, 95% within ±2σ and 99.7% within ±3σ.
According to Herzberg's two-factor theory, salary and working conditions are:
Motivators that create high job satisfaction
Hygiene factors whose absence causes dissatisfaction
Herzberg separated hygiene factors (prevent dissatisfaction) from motivators like achievement and recognition.
The highest level in Maslow's hierarchy of needs is:
Maslow's order is physiological, safety, social, esteem and, at the top, self-actualisation.
A borrower has current assets of ₹400 lakh and current liabilities other than bank borrowings of ₹100 lakh. Under Tandon Committee's second method of lending, MPBF is:
Method II: MPBF = 75% of CA − CL = 0.75 × 400 − 100 = 300 − 100 = ₹200 lakh.
Under the Nayak Committee (turnover) method, a MSME borrower with projected annual turnover of ₹2 crore should get working capital bank finance of at least:
WC requirement is 25% of turnover, of which bank finance is at least 20% of turnover = 0.20 × 2 crore = ₹40 lakh (margin 5%).
A project's cash available for debt service (PAT + depreciation + interest) is ₹30 lakh and its debt obligations (interest + principal instalments) are ₹20 lakh. The DSCR is:
DSCR = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5, meaning cash flows cover debt service 1.5 times.
Compliance risk in a bank refers to:
The risk of a fall in share prices
The risk of legal or regulatory sanctions, financial loss or reputational damage from failure to comply with laws, rules and standards
The risk of borrowers prepaying loans
The risk arising only from foreign exchange movements
Compliance risk arises from non-adherence to laws, regulations and codes of conduct, and is managed by an independent compliance function.
A 360-degree performance appraisal gathers feedback from:
Superiors, peers, subordinates and sometimes customers
360-degree appraisal uses multiple raters around the employee for a rounded assessment.
Higher deposits every March and October due to festivals and financial-year closing, repeating each year, illustrate which component of a time series?
Seasonal variations are regular patterns recurring within a year; cycles span several years.
A bank has Tier 1 capital of ₹900 crore, Tier 2 capital of ₹300 crore and risk-weighted assets of ₹10,000 crore. Its CRAR is:
A loan of ₹200 crore carrying a 75% risk weight adds how much to risk-weighted assets?
Under RBI's Basel III framework, the minimum total capital ratio including the Capital Conservation Buffer is:
RBI requires minimum total capital of 9% plus a CCB of 2.5%, i.e., 11.5% (higher than the Basel minimum of 8% + 2.5%).
The Liquidity Coverage Ratio requires banks to hold high-quality liquid assets at least equal to:
100% of total net cash outflows over the next 30 days under stress
25% of net cash outflows over one year
LCR = HQLA ÷ net cash outflows over 30 stress days, with a minimum of 100%.
A bank has rate-sensitive assets of ₹500 crore and rate-sensitive liabilities of ₹700 crore in a time bucket. If interest rates rise by 1%, its net interest income will approximately:
A bond has Macaulay duration of 5 years and yield of 10%. For a 1% rise in yield, its price will fall by approximately:
If USD/INR is 84.00 and EUR/USD is 1.10, the EUR/INR cross rate is:
Spot USD/INR is 83.00 and the 3-month forward rate is 83.50. The annualised forward premium on USD is approximately:
A foreign bank's rupee account with an Indian bank
An Indian bank's account in foreign currency maintained with a bank abroad
An account maintained with RBI for CRR
Nostro means 'our account with you'; a foreign bank's rupee account in India is a Vostro account.
Under Basel norms, operational risk is the risk of loss resulting from:
Inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems, or external events
Changes in the government's fiscal deficit
This is the Basel definition; it includes legal risk but excludes strategic and reputational risk.
Under UCP 600, banks dealing with a letter of credit:
Inspect the goods physically before payment
Must verify the quality of goods at the port
Deal with documents and not with the goods to which the documents relate
Are responsible for the buyer's commercial disputes
LC operations are document-based: payment depends on presentation of complying documents.
Under RBI's Basel III norms, the minimum leverage ratio for Domestic Systemically Important Banks is:
RBI prescribes a leverage ratio of 4% for D-SIBs and 3.5% for other scheduled commercial banks.
A trading portfolio has a 1-day VaR of ₹10 crore at 99% confidence. This means:
The portfolio can never lose more than ₹10 crore
The portfolio will lose ₹10 crore every day
There is a 99% chance of losing ₹10 crore
Losses exceeding ₹10 crore are expected on only about 1 day in 100
VaR is a threshold loss: at 99% confidence, a one-day loss larger than ₹10 crore should occur on about 1% of days.
When the price of a product rises by 10%, quantity demanded falls by 20%. The price elasticity of demand (absolute value) is:
Elasticity = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 (elastic demand).
A firm is financed 60% by equity costing 15% and 40% by debt costing 10% before tax. With a 25% tax rate, its WACC is:
A company has net profit margin of 5%, asset turnover of 2 times and equity multiplier of 2. Using DuPont analysis, its ROE is:
ROE = margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier = 5% × 2 × 2 = 20%.
A share will pay a dividend of ₹10 next year; the required return is 12% and growth is 7% forever. Its intrinsic value is:
Which of the following is NOT one of Porter's five competitive forces?
Porter's forces are rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, and the bargaining power of buyers and suppliers.
In the BCG matrix, a business with a high relative market share in a low-growth market is a:
Cash cows dominate mature markets and generate surplus cash that can fund other businesses.
A merger between two banks offering similar services in the same market is a:
Horizontal mergers combine firms at the same stage of the same industry; vertical ones combine supplier and buyer stages.
A company's NOPAT is ₹50 crore, capital employed is ₹300 crore and WACC is 12%. Its Economic Value Added is:
A firm has a contribution of ₹400 lakh and EBIT of ₹100 lakh. Its degree of operating leverage is:
DOL = contribution ÷ EBIT = 400 ÷ 100 = 4; a 1% change in sales changes EBIT by about 4%.
A situation of high inflation combined with stagnant output and high unemployment is called:
Stagflation combines stagnation in growth with rising prices, making policy choices difficult.
In a SWOT analysis, which elements relate to factors internal to the organisation?
Strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats come from the external environment.
According to Modigliani–Miller (without taxes), the value of a firm:
Is independent of its capital structure
In perfect markets without taxes, MM show that financing mix does not change firm value; only the assets' cash flows matter.
Under Section 5(b) of the Banking Regulation Act, 'banking' means accepting deposits of money from the public for the purpose of:
Lending or investment, repayable on demand or otherwise and withdrawable by cheque, draft, order or otherwise
This statutory definition centres on accepting public deposits for lending/investment that are repayable and withdrawable.
The power of RBI to issue directions to banking companies in public interest is contained in:
Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act
Section 35A empowers RBI to give directions to banks in the public interest, interest of depositors or banking policy.
Under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, a company cannot carry on banking business in India without:
Approval of the Ministry of Corporate Affairs alone
Section 22 requires every banking company to hold a licence issued by RBI.
Under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, the secured creditor gives the defaulting borrower a notice to discharge liabilities within:
If the borrower does not pay within 60 days of the demand notice, the lender may take measures under Section 13(4).
SARFAESI enforcement cannot be taken where the amount due is less than:
20% of the principal amount and interest thereon
Section 31(j) excludes cases where the dues are less than 20% of principal and interest.
The minimum amount of default required to initiate a corporate insolvency resolution process under the IBC is currently:
The threshold was raised from ₹1 lakh to ₹1 crore in 2020.
Including extensions and time spent in legal proceedings, the CIRP under the IBC must ordinarily be completed within:
The basic period is 180 days, extendable by 90 days, with an overall cap of 330 days including litigation time.
Banks can approach a Debts Recovery Tribunal for recovery of debts of:
The pecuniary threshold for DRT jurisdiction was raised from ₹10 lakh to ₹20 lakh in 2018.
Under the Limitation Act, the general period to file a suit for recovery of a loan is:
Most money-recovery suits must be filed within three years; 12 years applies to enforcing a mortgage.
Under PMLA rules, banks must report cash transactions to FIU-IND in a Cash Transaction Report when they exceed:
₹10 lakh (or its equivalent, including integrally connected series in a month)
CTRs cover cash transactions above ₹10 lakh and connected series aggregating above that within a month.
A Suspicious Transaction Report must be furnished to FIU-IND within:
7 days of arriving at the conclusion that the transaction is suspicious
PMLA rules require STRs within seven days of the bank concluding that a transaction is suspicious.
Customer complaints against RBI-regulated entities such as banks and NBFCs are now handled under:
The Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021
RB-IOS 2021 integrated the earlier banking, NBFC and digital transactions ombudsman schemes into one.
